title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: How Steadicams Work
summary: Rerun of the 2016 Stuff You Should Know episode on the Steadicam, released in the 2025 summer movie playlist. The hosts cover the history of the Steadicam, invented by Garrett Brown, who demonstrated it with a sizzle reel of previously impossible shots that drew attention in Hollywood, including a note from Stanley Kubrick about a shadow in the reel. Early films using it include Bound for Glory, Rocky, and Marathon Man, and later The Shining, Goodfellas, and Return of the Jedi. The episode explains the mechanics: a vest, a spring-and-pulley arm, and a sled with a gimbal that moves the center of gravity onto the pole, plus high and low mode. It also covers the cost and skill of operators, consumer stabilizers, and Garrett Brown's Skycam. The episode ends with listener mail from a Christian listener.

segments.title: Summer movie playlist intro
segments.summary: Chuck introduces the episode as part of the summer movie playlist, a rerun from June 2016 about the Steadicam.

segments.title: Opening banter and film industry experience
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Chuck's hat and patches, then discuss whether they have worked with Steadicams on set and how skilled Steadicam operators are.

segments.title: Pre-Steadicam filming limits
segments.summary: Chuck notes Steadicam was commercially available the year he was born. The hosts explain that before it, impossible shots like stairs and rough terrain were hard to film with a dolly, and handheld shots were seen as avant garde.

segments.title: Garrett Brown and the human balance system
segments.summary: The hosts introduce Garrett Brown, who was working on TV commercials and Sesame Street in Philadelphia. They discuss how the human inner ear and retina offset motion, which the Steadicam aimed to reproduce.

segments.title: Dollies and the Brown Stabilizer
segments.summary: The hosts explain how a dolly works and its limits on rough terrain and stairs. Brown set out to invent something better, first calling it the Brown Stabilizer before renaming it Steadicam.

segments.title: Sizzle reel and Kubrick's shadow warning
segments.summary: Brown made a sizzle reel of thirty impossible shots without showing how they were done, and it spread through Hollywood. Stanley Kubrick warned him that shadows in two shots revealed the rig, and Brown removed them in a second edition.

segments.title: Rocky steps shot and early Steadicam films
segments.summary: The Philadelphia Museum of Art steps shot from the reel inspired John Avildsen to use it in Rocky. The hosts note Bound for Glory and Marathon Man as early Steadicam films, and Brown's 1977 patent and 1978 Academy Award.

segments.title: Hosts on Rocky and other movies
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Rocky as a love story and the later sequels, and touch on Martin Scorsese's new gangster film with De Niro, Pacino and Pesci, and Jack Nicholson's performance in The Wolf of Wall Street.

segments.title: How the Steadicam works: vest, arm, and sled
segments.summary: The hosts describe the three parts of the Steadicam: a vest, a spring arm attached to it, and a sled holding the camera. The arm uses springs and a cable and pulley tension system to offset the camera's weight, and the camera can be in high or low mode. The hosts mention a homemade version built by Josh's brother.

segments.title: Gimbal, center of gravity, and moment of inertia
segments.summary: The hosts explain the gimbal, how Brown spread the camera's mass along the pole to move the center of gravity to the pole, and how moment of inertia affects steadiness. They compare it to balancing a broomstick on a finger and say the arm isolates the operator's movement.

segments.title: Weight changes and operator fatigue
segments.summary: The hosts note that the balance can shift during filming as film or the digital card changes. They describe Steadicam operators taking breaks because the rig is heavy on the chest.

segments.title: Eurovision Steadicam shot
segments.summary: Chuck describes a Eurovision shot in which a Steadicam operator on a Segway circled a singer, and the hosts comment on the video quality.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Ad break.

segments.title: The Shining and Kubrick's use of Steadicam
segments.summary: Kubrick was a fan and worked with Brown on The Shining, with the two clashing on set. The hosts discuss the tricycle hallway shots and how they might have been filmed.

segments.title: Goodfellas and lighting long shots
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the Copacabana single take in Goodfellas, which follows characters through the back halls and kitchen. They note the difficulty of lighting such a long continuous shot.

segments.title: Return of the Jedi speeder bike shot
segments.summary: The speeder bike chase in Return of the Jedi was filmed with Steadicam, with Brown walking through Redwood National Park and the footage sped up.

segments.title: Speeding up footage and consumer stabilizers
segments.summary: Chuck explains that sped-up film exaggerates small movements, so smooth Steadicam footage was needed. Josh notes that consumer Steadicam-style stabilizers are now affordable.

segments.title: Consumer stabilizers, gimbals, and drones
segments.summary: The hosts mention a GoPro stabilizer and the Smoothie for iPhone, along with gimbal-based drone stabilizers. They joke about a cereal mascot, then turn to the Steadicam brand.

segments.title: Steadicam manufacturers and Skycam
segments.summary: Tiffen makes Steadicam. The hosts mention competitors Glidecam and Varizoom, dolly makers Chapman and Fisher, and Garrett Brown's later invention, the Skycam.

segments.title: Camera positions: missionary and Don Juan
segments.summary: Josh describes film set slang for camera positions, which he calls missionary and Don Juan. Chuck signs off with the HowStuffWorks search suggestion.

segments.title: Listener mail: encouragement from a Christian listener
segments.summary: Dane in Minnesota writes that he appreciates how the show treats religious topics, including Easter traditions and satanic panic.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Chuck gives social media and email contact info and the website. Josh closes by pointing to HowStuffWorks for more topics.
